extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of humor studies, folklore, anthropology, linguistics, psychology, and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and analytic criteria for studying jokes and joking: theoretical frameworks, genre distinctions, performance context, aesthetics, and sociopolitical dimensions as presented in a scholarly book overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Oring developed his formulation of “appropriate incongruity” as a frame to understand what jokes must do to produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a central criterion for when a joke produces humor; it is tested against other major theoretical positions in the field. (Verbatim phrase from the book summary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Parsing the Joke: the general theory of verbal humor is treated as a core approach to analyzing joke structure and mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used alongside appropriate incongruity to parse how verbal jokes produce comedic effects (referenced in chapter heading and book summary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual Integration Theory (Blending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual integration theory (also called blending) is presented as a major position for explaining humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explored in the book (chapter: 'Blending and Humor') as an account of how merged conceptual spaces can produce comedic meaning and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Benign violation theory is listed as one of the principal contemporary approaches tested against appropriate incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a competing explanatory framework for when violations are perceived as humorous rather than offensive, per book summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: False-Belief Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: False-belief theory is treated as a theoretical lens for understanding aspects of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned among the major positions the author tests; implies assessing jokes by whether they exploit others' false beliefs or perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and Evolution of Jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about the construction and evolution of jokes are posed as basic analytic concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks how jokes are built and how they change over time; this frames comparative and historical analysis of joke forms and transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Joke Targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Untangling who the actual targets of a joke might be is identified as an important analytical task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzing a joke includes determining explicit and implicit targets (victims, institutions, ideas), which affects interpretation and ethics of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic Qualities and Aesthetics of Jokes and Performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize the artistic qualities of jokes and joke performances; treat jokes as objects of aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book emphasizes aesthetics (chapters: 'From the Ridiculous to the Sublime: Jokes and Art' and 'Contested Performance and Joke Aesthetics'), suggesting criteria for evaluating artistry, taste, and form in jokes and performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing Effects (e.g., 'Framing Borat')
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing—how a comic persona or media context presents a joke/performance—matters for interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 'Framing Borat' indicates that the way a joke or character is framed by context or media alters its reception and meaning; framing is thus an analytic criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Risk and Repressive Contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing political jokes under repressive regimes: the riskiness and consequences of joking about politics is a key dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 'Risky Business: Political Jokes under Repressive Regimes' highlights that political context, censorship, and danger shape both content and function of jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and Medium Effects (Internet/List Jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Format- and medium-specific forms (e.g., list jokes and jokes on the Internet) require particular analytic attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 'Listing toward Lists: Jokes on the Internet' implies that digital forms and list-based structures have distinct mechanics and evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Joke Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and analyze what constitutes a narrative joke as a distinct form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 'What Is a Narrative Joke?' indicates attention to plot, timing, and narrative mechanics as criteria for evaluating narrative jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural-Specific Analysis (e.g., the Jewish Joke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demythologizing culturally specific joke traditions (such as the Jewish joke) is a substantive analytic concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 'Demythologizing the Jewish Joke' suggests criteria for evaluating cultural narratives, stereotypes, and historicization in joke traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/Theoretical Reappraisal (e.g., Freud on Jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-examining historical theories of humor (what Freud actually said about jokes) is part of methodological critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 'What Freud Actually Said about Jokes' signals the importance of accurately interpreting and testing legacy theories as criteria for scholarly rigor.
